title: Ming Dynasty statue unearthed in WA back in Chinese hands
text:
A Ming Dynasty Buddha statue discovered by two prospectors beside a remote highway in WA has been formally handed over to Chinese officials.

Indigenous readers are advised that this story contains the name of a person who has died.

Leon Deschamps and Shayne Thomson were testing prospecting equipment on a roadside in the Shark Bay region in 2018 when their instruments made the distinctive tone indicating the presence of precious metals.

The prospectors were recording as they unearthed the rare 15-centimetre bronze statue from beneath 20cm of topsoil.

The infant Buddha statue is at least 500 years old. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

After spending considerable time and money investigating the Buddha, the pair advocated for it to be formally returned to the Chinese government as a gesture of peace and goodwill.

It was formally handed over to Chinese consular representatives in an emotional ceremony at the Denham foreshore this morning.

"This is a story that not many Australians know and we feel proud to share it," Mr Deschamps said.

At the ceremony Mr Deschamps and Mr Thomson honoured their late friend, Malgana man Nick Pedrocchi. They had promised him they would ensure the Buddha's safe passage home.

The Buddha was handed to representatives from the Chinese consulate in a ceremony on the Denham foreshore. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"I remember the moment we passed the Buddha into Nick's hands … the instant he held it, his body got covered in goosebumps," Mr Deschamps said.

"We are not religious men, but there has been a very spiritual element to this.

"It's been very Yin and Yang today. There's been joy and sadness — joy in knowing Buddha is going back to people who will treat it property, and sadness thinking about Nick.

" But mostly I have this great sense of relief off my shoulders. We did the thing we told our brother we would do. "

The Buddha will return to China with red dirt from Shark Bay, as well as a golden pearl shell.

Consul Guannan Liu (left) and Acting Consul-General Wang Fengzhong (holding statue) with Shayne Thompson and Leon Deschamps. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Australia China Friendship Society WA president Simon Wu said the repatriation of the Buddha was an incredibly generous and significant gesture.

"Today is an example of how we can bring cultures, countries and people together through a small object. It's showing respect and goodwill," he said.

"For something like this to come home, for the Chinese people in China, they will be happy and welcoming.

"When it starts its new journey in China it will always be connected back to Shark Bay, so that our next generation can learn about how the Australian people and Chinese people have a friendship that can continue for generations."

Representatives of the Chinese government flew to Shark Bay for the official handover ceremony. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Statue's history still a mystery

Asian art expert Lee Young verified the Buddha dated back to the Ming Dynasty, a period of rule in China from 1368 to 1644 recognised for its trade and architecture.

Such statues were used in ceremonies to celebrate Buddha's birthday. Water was poured over its shoulders while people recited the mantra to do good deeds, speak good words and think good thoughts.

Exactly how the Buddha came to be in Shark Bay is unknown, but there are some theories. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

But Mr Deschamps and Mr Thomson never definitively solved the mystery of who left the statue in Shark Bay and why they were there.

The pair even worked with the Shipwreck Hunters Australia TV program to explore the theory that it came from a Ming treasure ship.

They say it is more likely linked to the beginnings of WA's pearling industry, which was pioneered, in part, by Chinese people in the 1850s.

The prospectors want to see a monument erected to acknowledge Shark Bay's pearling history. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Pearlers used Malay, Chinese and Aboriginal people as labourers, but eventually Chinese people established their own operations and camps in the region.

"Shark Bay, for 100 years, was a pearling port. At times there was more Chinese here than Europeans," Mr Thompson said.

"They lived here, they worked here, they died here.

"I think bridge is the perfect metaphor to use with this. Today the bridge was everybody coming together with the same feeling and passion we are feeling, and it is a little metal object that has brought us together."

Mr Deschamps and Mr Thomson are calling for a monument to be erected in the region to acknowledge Shark Bay as the birthplace of WA's pearling industry.

title: Eleven Edge Early Learning centres to close after failing to find buyers
text:
Eleven childcare centres of the collapsed Edge Early Learning group are shutting down with parents only finding out with 48 hours' notice.

Seven of the centres are in Queensland, three in South Australia and one in the ACT.

The closures are happening after Edge Early Learning tumbled into voluntary administration in August this year, amid tough times for operators in the childcare sector.

Administrators KordaMentha successfully found buyers for 53 centres in Queensland and South Australia, including proposals for not-for-profit giant GoodStart Early Learning to acquire 31 facilities.

But despite attempts, acquirers could not be found for 11 centres that were deemed not viable to keep running.

Some parents only found out on Tuesday morning that centres would be closing as of late Wednesday.

A spokesman for KordaMentha said parents at affected centres were being advised in writing of potential nearby facilities where there was some availability for new enrolments.

KordaMentha administrator David Johnstone acknowledged the "impact that the closure of the 11 centres will have on staff as well as families and carers who now need to make alternate childcare arrangements".

title: Dying Queensland man wins record $1.9m payment after developing asbestosis
text:
A Mackay grandfather dying from the debilitating disease asbestosis has won Australia's largest-ever compensation payment on record after being awarded nearly $1.9 million dollars.

Robin Smith, now in his late 70s, developed asbestosis after exposure to dangerous silicate while working as a plumber from the mid-1960s onwards.

He was unwittingly exposed while working for the former Queensland Government's Mackay Harbour Board, now known as the North Queensland Bulk Ports Corporation Limited (NQBP).

Robin Smith was exposed to asbestos while working as a plumber. (Facebook: North Queensland Bulk Ports Corporation Limited)

As a plumber, his work involved using a demolition saw to cut into asbestos cement pipes when working on the water lines throughout the port, during 1981 and the mid 1990s.

The judgement was the first of its kind in Queensland.

Mr Smith did not want to speak publicly, but through his lawyer Slater and Gordon's Sean Sweeney, he said he hoped his win was a "watershed moment" for other victims.

'Pain and suffering' critical part of payment

The lawyer said it was significant because $800,000 of the judgement was awarded for "pain and suffering".

Asbestosis is a chronic lung condition caused by inhaling asbestos fibres, that can take 10 to 60 years to present.

It is a progressive, slow death over time; there is no cure.

The trial was held from August 17 to 20 this year against Amaca Pty Ltd (previously James Hardie & Coy), North Queensland Bulk Ports Corporation, and WorkCover Queensland for Mr Smith's earlier de-registered employers.

Asbestosis is a chronic lung condition caused by inhaling asbestos fibres. (ABC News)

Experts told the court that Mr Smith's asbestosis was progressive, irreversible, and was fatal and his life expectancy was around five to six years.

"Asbestosis is a devastating diagnosis. It's often a debilitating disease that progresses over a long period of time, taking a devastating toll on victims and their families," Mr Sweeney said.

"By the time Mr Smith dies from the condition he will have suffered from deteriorating respiratory symptoms for over a decade.

"This judgement serves as a critical reminder about the dangers of asbestos.

"The fact that Mr Smith experienced such extreme asbestos exposure into the 1990s is deeply concerning."

Separate historic case

The law firm had previously won another historic case involving a WA man, Kim Martin, for issues also related to asbestos, after he contracted mesothelioma, an incurable terminal cancer.

In 2024 the court found he had been exposed to asbestos in James Hardie products while working in factories in Western Australia and Queensland in the 1960s and 1970s.

Kim Martin received $1.2 million after developing mesothelioma. (Supplied)

Mr Martin won a payout of $1.2 million, nearly $700,000 less than this week's win for Mr Smith.

As far back as 2018 James Hardie was accused of playing hardball with victims for allegedly not meeting compensation obligations and restricting asbestos payments to dying victims.

According to the Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency (ASEA) at that time, the number of Australians with asbestos diseases, was currently about 4,000 a year, and rising.

Asbestos was banned in Australia two decades ago, but there remains more than six million tonnes of the dangerous material in buildings across the country.

"Secondly it keeps the conversation going about the dangers, it is still in our homes and schools", Mr Smith said.

From home renovations to the uncovering of asbestos in mulch at schools across the country, the once popular product still haunts communities.

Just in July an area from a WA school was cordoned off due to dangers.

Asbestos was banned in Australia two decades ago. (ABC News: Claire Moodie)

Mr Sweeney said his law firm was now seeing cases related to trades people who worked with new asbestos products before they started to be phased out in the 1980's and more recently through the 90s and 2000's others exposed through home renovations.

He stressed it was a legally fraught area due to issues about liability and between employers and manufacturers was "making these claims more complicated".

Sean Sweeney said Mr Smith's win was a "watershed moment" for victims.

"So decisions like this latest one can provide guidance for people pursuing compensation and also lawyers working in this space."

In a statement Mr Smith's former employer NQBP said: "First and foremost, our thoughts are with Mr Smith and his family."

"We respect the Supreme Court's findings but due to the nature of the case and other parties involved it is not appropriate for us to comment in detail," the statement added.

title: How NRL's Super League bid could revive a fallen giant
text:
As talks over the NRL's proposed investment in Super League near the pointy end of negotiations, Trent Robinson says a partnership between the two competitions could help reinvigorate the sport in France.

After guiding the Sydney Roosters to the fourth NRL premiership victory of his tenure earlier this month, Robinson would have every right to be sat somewhere in the south of France with his feet up sipping a glass of red.

But instead he finds himself offering his services to the French national team, where he supports head coach Laurent Frayssinous as director of rugby, in preparation for Friday's World Cup opener against Samoa.

On the other side of the world, club owners in England and the Super League's two French sides — Catalans Dragons and Toulouse Olympique — are weighing up an offer that would lead to the NRL providing an investment into the code's only other professional competition.

NRL's Super League investment offer Britain's Super League has revealed it has received an investment offer from the NRL, taking Australian involvement in British rugby league's premier tournament a significant step closer.

Some British clubs are reluctant to cede power to the NRL but Robinson is a firm believer in how Australia can help revive France as an international force.

"I think the NRL will have a world vision of rugby league, and I know they see the value of French rugby league and the importance of it," the Roosters coach told AAP.

"I think it would continue the progression of having a place at the table."

France was one of the sport's leading powers in the 1950s and 1960s but their stock has fallen considerably.

The presence of two French clubs in Super League, from which the majority of the national team is drawn, has so far failed to translate into international success.

France was supposed to host this year's World Cup until the government pulled the pin, citing the expense of hosting rugby union's World Cup in 2023 and the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Ranked 11th in the world, France are seen as $21 outsiders by bookmakers for their meeting with a Samoan team laden with NRL talent at CommBank Stadium.

Mitchell Pearce, who has retired in France after playing for Catalans, said: "There's some great French talent and they'll be enjoying the opportunity (to play in the World Cup).

Samoa plans World Cup tilt With the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup officially launched, Samoa are looking to repeat their fairytale run to the 2022 final.

"I think it'd be great for the NRL to expand and open up French rugby league and help the development pathways."

France's struggles to field a strong international side, they were hammered 62-4 by Samoa four years ago, can surely be attributed to the fact their clubs are operating in the most cash-rich market in any rugby code.

France's top rugby union competition, the Top14, has a salary cap of roughly $18 million, the NRL's is around $12 million, while the Super League's is approaching $4 million.

"There's a respect that is growing in France for rugby league from when I first went 24 years ago," Robinson said.

"It's because we've got a great sport and because of the Catalans and Toulouse.

"It's a fair mountain to climb, the Top 14, and trying to catch up with that.

"But it (league) does have respect and the NRL would add to that because there's an enormous amount of respect for it in rugby union circles."

AAP

title: Examining WA's proposed university merger, and why it's causing concern
text:
The Western Australian government wants to merge three of its public universities — the University of Western Australia, Curtin University and Murdoch University.

But this week's announcement that a business case is being developed has raised a host of questions about the impact on students, staff, the economy and taxpayers.

Murdoch University would be merged with Curtin and the University of Western Australia under the plan. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

What's behind the merger?

The government argues a merger would greatly benefit the state and create a "once-in-a-generation opportunity".

WA Premier Roger Cook says it would provide maximum economic benefit for the state, improve outcomes for students, boost research funding, retain and attract students and address low degree completion rates.

WA moves ahead with university merger plans Premier Roger Cook says a potential merger could create a "once-in-a-generation" opportunity as all three universities raise concerns about the move.

Education Minister Tony Buti says the state currently has "duplicated offerings, fragmented investment and limited scale across our universities".

He says WA's universities are in a "race to the bottom" and the reforms are necessary to ensure the sector is "world-class".

How will it work?

Many of the specifics remain unclear, but it's anticipated it would lead to a "mega-university" of almost 120,000 students.

Murdoch University has a highly regarded veterinary medicine program. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

The universities say that is a scale unmatched in Australia and rare internationally, while the government argues it would keep the sector competitive and attract more students and investment.

Details about a potential name or campus arrangements are not yet known.

While the government suggests the move would make the tertiary education system more financially efficient, there are no assurances it would lead to cheaper degrees.

The University of Western Australia says any merger must deliver "significant benefits" to students and the state. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

"The critical question — what will this actually cost the taxpayers, who they expect to foot the bill if they take this up — is still unanswered," shadow education minister Liam Staltari said.

The merger does not affect Edith Cowan University, which last year moved into a new $853 million CBD campus, or Notre Dame in Fremantle.

What are the unis saying?

Curtin's vice-chancellor Harlene Hayne expressed "deep concern" and claimed it was a costly process to "fix something that is not broken".

Uni merger 'solves problems we don't have': Curtin Curtin University's vice-chancellor describes a proposed merger of three WA universities as a "solution looking for a problem".

She said Curtin would "vigorously oppose" a potential amalgamation, saying it "solves problems we don't have and creates problems we don't need".

Murdoch's VC Andrew Deeks was equally critical, saying the merger would "absolutely not" give WA students a better education.

Meanwhile, UWA struck a more neutral tone, with its VC Amit Chakma praising the state government's "strategic direction", while stopping short of endorsing the proposal as a whole.

"My support is based on aspirations. It has nothing to do with our current-day [financial] situation," he told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Professor Amit Chakma is the Vice-Chancellor of The University of Western Australia. (Supplied: Twitter)

"Are there issues? Of course there are issues. But the aspiration is based off what Western Australia can be 10 years, 20 years, 30 years from now, and what role universities can play in that."

What are students saying?

Students are expressing concern, with some claiming it fails to take their interests into account.

Curtin law and international relations student Ebony Whitney told the ABC she feared a merger could significantly disrupt current students.

There are fears students could suffer a loss of choice and fall through the cracks if the merger goes ahead. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"It's pretty scary, to be completely honest," she said.

"I'll have Curtin on my certificate, and down the track employers look at where you studied. If that institution doesn't exist any more, it's going to be quite a bad look."

Graduates' satisfaction with degrees at record lows Australian students are less satisfied with their university degrees than ever before, according to a long-running survey.

Curtin Student Guild president Dylan Storer fears students could fall through the cracks in a much larger university.

"It's the loss of choice, it's the monopolisation of … tertiary education here in Western Australia, it's reducing options, but also reducing that diversity that is really important," he said.

Is this about land?

The three campuses sit on large plots of land in the Perth metropolitan area, close to transport links.

The premier suggested selling off some of that land could help pay for the merger.

"We believe that this should be not up to the WA taxpayer to foot all the bill. The universities have got resources and significant parcels of land ... land which could be repurposed for housing," Roger Cook said.

Separately, the government is looking to redevelop the old ECU campus in Mt Lawley into a new inner-city neighbourhood over the next 15 years.

Has it been done anywhere else?

WA appears to be following the lead of South Australia, which merged the University of South Australia and University of Adelaide to create Adelaide University.

The Adelaide University merger has left students frustrated over enrolments and study plans. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

That university opened its doors in January and was projected to be one of the larger higher education institutions in the nation, with modelling suggesting it would bring $500 million to the state's economy each year.

However, a report last month found the new amalgamated university was not on track to meet its international student targets and is staring down tens of millions in lost revenue.

What happens next?

The government will carry out the business case with input from a steering committee chaired by Mark Barnaba.

Mark Barnaba is leading the steering committee set to advise the government on the merger. (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

Mr Barnaba says a merger would be good for the state and has dismissed suggestions it would result in job cuts.

Meanwhile, more than two-thirds of WA university staff surveyed by the National Tertiary Education Union oppose the merger, with the union vowing to vehemently fight the proposal.

The findings of the business case are set to be presented by the middle of 2027, the government says.

title: Minister says child safety has 'stabilised' despite drop in urgent cases seen on time
text:
Nine in ten children in urgent need of state care were not helped on time in the past four months, according to new child safety figures.

Quarterly performance data showed at risk children that needed to be assessed within three days had not been seen-to within that timeframe.

Minister Camm said the department had experienced more notifications.

"That is putting demand on our frontline staff," she said.

"We want people to notify if there is a child at risk of harm. We want to encourage that."

That number has moved backward from a year ago, when nearly three quarters of children requiring assessment within three days were not seen on time.

Opposition leader Steven Miles said responding to at risk children should be the government's focus.

Steven Miles said the government should not be excited by these figures. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"These are children that are already traumatised. Imagine what this must feel like for them," he said.

"The minister shouldn't be excited, she should be ashamed."

Residential care system has 'stabilised'

In her first week back after six weeks of medical leave, Queensland Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm spruiked the quarterly reporting.

The number of children placed in residential care had decreased over the last three months to 2,804 children, 15 fewer kids than in the last reporting period.

"Residential care was established to be the care of last resort. For the first time, the numbers have decreased. Small, but they have stabilised," Minister Camm said.

Amanda Camm returned to work from medical leave this week. (ABC News)

There was a slight uptick in the number of children in foster care and kinship care.

Minister Camm said the government would continue to reform the system and recruit more carers.

"While we acknowledge it is a modest movement, it is recognition that we have stabilised the system," she said.

The government also reported that the average number of cases per child safety office was "remaining stable" at 15.9.

Together Union assistant secretary Dee Spink. (ABC News)

Dee Spink is the Assistant Secretary of Together Union, which represents child safety workers.

She said these figures don't match what their members on the front line are reporting.

"It really is so far from the reality of what our members tell us they're dealing with every day," she said.

"Our members in child safety are working so hard, they go above and beyond, they hours they're not paid for but we know that there's still plenty of vacant child safety roles across the state."

Government promises further change on the way

Queensland parliament is set to pass a bill this week that would establish a centralised agency aimed at improving the protection of children from sexual abuse.

It was a response to an inquiry prompted by the offending of paedophile Ashley Paul Griffith, which found multiple opportunities had been missed to prevent his offending.

The bill, expected to pass parliament this week, would establish the Child Protection Commission, bringing together different agencies responsible for child safety matters under one banner.

Queensland Family and Child Commission Chief Executive Luke Twyford said he welcomed the changes.

Queensland Family and Child Commission Chief Executive Luke Twyford said responsibility for child safety extended beyond government. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"[It] will change my current role and I'm happy about that because having sat with the victims, the parents, the police officers, the councillors, the current system is clearly not okay," he said.

"Queensland is taking a big step."

title: Victorian firefighters' union threatens legal action against own members
text:
The Victorian firefighters' union is threatening legal action against its own members for not paying a $644 levy to cover its hefty legal costs.

In what some firefighters have called a "ridiculous" move, the union last year resolved to charge all members the fee to cover the union's legal bills which financial reports show ran to almost $2.3 million last financial year.

The levy is on top of union membership fees, which are more than $2,000 per year for senior firefighters.

Letters sent by law firm Slater and Gordon notify members who have not paid the levy that if the matter is not resolved, court proceedings will be commenced against them to recover the debt.

"If proceedings are commenced, in addition to being required to pay the CCF [Court Case Funding] levy, you may also be ordered to pay interest and costs," the letter says.

One union member and senior firefighter, speaking to the ABC on the condition of anonymity, said the union should be supporting members, not attacking them.

"[It's] unhelpful and detrimental to the mental health and wellbeing of our people," he said.

He also questioned whether the cost of using a legal firm to recover the debt would actually outstrip the cost of the debt itself.

A Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) employee told the ABC they couldn't believe the union would send a legal letter to its own members, and that one recipient had been in tears over the potential action.

Union secretary Peter Marshall says every member who received a legal letter was contacted several times first. (ABC News: Stephanie Anderson)

United Firefighters Union (UFU) Victoria branch secretary Peter Marshall said in a statement the decision to impose the levy was made by members over five union meetings, and carried unanimously.

"Most members expected the request and have already paid," he said. "No member received a legal letter out of the blue. Every one of them was contacted several times first. "If there are any other members who have financial or other struggles, it is well known that I can be reached at any time, and their circumstances will be dealt with sensitivity and in confidence."

The union would not say how many letters have been sent, though the FRV staff member said they were aware of more than 40.

Union spends more than $10m in legal fees over six years

Over the past six years, the Victorian branch of the union has spent more than $10 million on legal fees, according to its own financial statements.

The current legal levy is to pay for ongoing action the union is taking against FRV in the Fair Work Commission over the firefighters' Enterprise Bargaining Agreement (EBA), according to firefighters who spoke to the ABC.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Jessica Longbottom at jessicalongbottom@protonmail.com. If you're sharing sensitive information, read our tips on how to contact us confidentially.

The parties have been unable to resolve the EBA since 2021, with FRV making the union seven separate offers over that time.

The Fair Work case is just one of several legal actions the union had underway.

The levy is to pay for ongoing action against Fire Rescue Victoria. (Source: Facebook/Fire Rescue Victoria)

The UFU and Mr Marshall also mounted Supreme Court action against the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) this year, trying to stop the public release of a report that examined former Labor ministers and the union secretary.

The bid ultimately failed, with the report published in August finding Mr Marshall was able to exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations for the 2016 firefighters EBA and was given privileged access to senior government figures.

This included holding secret meetings with the then-special minister of state, Gavin Jennings, to thrash out a deal, unknown to the then-Emergency Services Minister Jane Garrett, who opposed the union's demands.

At the time the IBAC report was handed down, Mr Marshall said he did not regret anything he had done to stand up for UFU members.

The union also has several other matters against FRV in the Fair Work Commission.

Several FRV employees told the ABC that the number of legal cases being pursued by the union was a point of frustration.

"If the union and its leadership had managed its money better and had not been so litigious, the members themselves wouldn't have to stump up for these additional costs," a senior firefighter told the ABC.

It's the second time the union has charged extra fees to members on top of their dues because of the union's legal bills.

Between 2014 and 2018, it charged members $500 a year to cover the union's legal costs against the Napthine Liberal government.

title: ACCC takes egg 'cartel' to court
text:
Australia's competition regulator has launched legal action against some of the country's biggest egg producers, alleging "cartel conduct" and other anti-competitive behaviour.

Sunny Queen, the largest egg supplier in Australia, and 11 other producers and suppliers are alleged to have breached competition laws by coordinating on the production and supply of eggs since 2020.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) filed civil proceedings in the Federal Court today, alleging the companies had coordinated on a range of decisions.

The ACCC alleges that since at least October 2020, the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on a range of business decisions, including buying a property in Queensland to stop a rival supplier acquiring it.

The legal filing comes more than a year since the ACCC launched court action against several large vegetable producers, alleging they formed a price-fixing cartel in supplying supermarket Aldi.

Producers and suppliers named

The ACCC alleges the egg suppliers and producers coordinated on decisions about production volumes, distribution, expansion plans and culling to manage perceived oversupply in a way that likely "substantially reduced competition for many years".

ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said eggs were an important household staple, and the alleged behaviour could result in less competitive prices for consumers.

"When you have good functioning competition then you have more choice, you also have price competition, so lower prices," she told Victorian Country Hour.

"Our concern is that when parties are not competing and they start working together … consumers can ultimately miss out.

Gina Cass-Gottlieb says the ACCC is concerned consumers could miss out on lower prices. (Four Corners: Rob Hill)

" This alleged conduct is extremely serious. "

Sunny Queen is Australia's largest wholesale egg supplier, holding about one-third of the market for supply of eggs to retailers such as Woolworths, Coles, Metcash, Aldi and Costco.

The company has warehouse and distribution facilities in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia.

The proceedings involve allegations against entities including Sunny Queen, Doug Hall Poultry Pty Ltd, Alpair Pty Ltd trading as McLean Farms, Ellerslie Free Range Farms Pty Ltd and Kinross Farm Pty Ltd along with seven other companies.

Farm sale examined

The ACCC alleges Sunny Queen, Hall and McLean Farms's coordination extended to purchasing a property in Pittsworth, Queensland, to prevent rival egg suppliers acquiring it.

"We also allege this had the effect of substantially lessening competition," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said.

Loading...

The competition regulator also alleged Sunny Queen restricted how many eggs its rival Kinross could sell to customers, and prevented Kinross from selling its eggs to Coles, Woolworths, Aldi, Metcash or Costco.

A spokesperson for Sunny Queen denied all allegations.

"Sunny Queen has cooperated fully with the ACCC throughout the course of its investigation," the spokesperson said.

" Sunny Queen denies the allegations and intends to defend the proceedings. "

The company said the allegations related to the terms of its agreements with its shareholders and main egg suppliers in Queensland and Victoria. It said it would remain "business as usual" while the matter was before the courts.

Doug Hall Poultry, McLean Farms, Kinross Farm, Yallamundi Farms and Ellerslie have been contacted for comment.

Sunny Queen is one of 12 egg producers named in the Federal Court matter. (Supplied)

Anti-competitive conduct

It is the first case the ACCC has brought involving concerted practice allegations since the prohibition was introduced in 2017.

A concerted practice involves cooperation between businesses that goes beyond them acting independently in response to market conditions.

"It can involve competitors coordinating their behaviour in ways that harm competition, even if there's no formal agreement," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said.

"It can involve communication between competitors, as we allege here, a regular exchange of information … in ways that reduce independent decision-making."

The ACCC alleges the egg industry is highly concentrated, with a small number of large suppliers and significant barriers to entry and expansion.

Eggs are a household staple, with Australians eating an average of more than 250 each a year, according to the ACCC.

title: Jetstar passenger plane and van nearly collide on airport tarmac
text:
A near miss between a Jetstar flight and a vehicle on the tarmac is being investigated by authorities after a series of incidents at a north Queensland airport.

The Airbus A320 was approaching Townsville Airport from Brisbane on October 7 when the pilots noticed a white van near the edge of the runway.

The plane passed over the van with about 15 metres' clearance.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) is investigating the near miss, which it has labelled a "serious incident".

In a statement, Jetstar said the flight landed normally and without incident.

"Safety is our number one priority, and we are working with the ATSB to understand the circumstances surrounding this incident," a spokesperson said.

Jetstar has confirmed the flight landed without incident. (Supplied)

Townsville Airport is owned by Queensland Airports Limited but operates as a joint user facility under an agreement with the Australian Defence Force.

Air traffic control services at the airport are provided by the Australian Air Force.

"Defence is working closely with the ATSB regarding its investigation into a runway incursion and near-collision at RAAF Base Townsville/Townsville Airport on 7 October 2026, after a vehicle entered a restricted airside area," a department spokesperson said.

"As this matter is under investigation, Defence will make no further comment at this time."

Several ongoing investigations

The recent near miss follows several serious incidents at Sydney Airport in recent months, including one the ATSB said was one of the most severe runway incidents in more than 20 years.

Sydney runway conflict 'severe' The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) has delivered findings on four of the six ongoing investigations into conflict investigations at Sydney Airport in recent months.

It is also the fourth incident the ATSB is investigating in or near Townsville Airport in the past two months.

On September 5, a Jetstar flight had been scheduled to take off from Townsville to Brisbane when the crew identified a performance calculation error — where the wrong numbers, settings or weight data had been used to calculate essential flight information.

In a separate incident on September 23, a Qantas flight from Brisbane to Townsville issued a mayday call due to low fuel levels after three missed landings because of poor visibility.

Meanwhile, a near-collision on October 1, about 18 kilometres west of Townsville Airport, is also being investigated as a "serious incident".

According to the ATSB investigation summary, in that incident a de Havilland DHC-8 (Dash 8) and a two-seater Aeroprakt A22LS were both in communication with the Townsville approach controller but did not see each other until they were about 1km apart.

They were about 500m apart before the Dash-8 dropped to a lower altitude to avoid a collision.

Searching for cause

Sidney Dekker, from Griffith University's Safety Science Innovation Lab, said there was only cause for concern if there was a common cause behind the incidents.

"Once we know what the ATSB comes up with in their investigation, then we'll have a better view of the extent to which it is connected to longstanding issues at Townsville or other airports across Australia," he said.

"Before they're done with that, there's really no basis for us to speculate about the cause."

Sidney Dekker says it is unlikely there is a common cause behind the recent incidents at Townsville Airport. (Supplied: Sidney Dekker)

Dr Dekker said the near miss involving the van was "serious enough to have a closer look at" and a "fairly rare" incident.

He said it was reassuring an accident had not actually happened.

"The system worked," he said.

"It came down to the final line of defence — if that's how you want to put it — that the pilots saw the van and went, 'Yeah right, we're not landing where this thing is sitting'. That is exactly what the system is supposed to do."

The ATSB will hand down reports on each incident after its investigation.

title: Alderman seeking re-election suspended for allegedly touching female staff
text:
A Tasmanian council alderman who is seeking re-election engaged in inappropriate behaviour, including touching female council employees, according to a report made public this week.

A local government code of conduct panel investigated a complaint made against Glenorchy City Council Alderman Peter Ridler last year by the council's former chief executive, Tony McMullen.

"It had come to his [Mr McMullen's] attention that a number of female workers were distressed after interactions with Ald Ridler," the panel's determination report reads.

The panel, comprised of Lynn Mason, Philip Cocker and David Palmer, found Alderman Ridler breached the council code of conduct on several days in November and December 2024 by:

A physical approach to a female staff member when she was adjusting the fan in a committee room, during which he allegedly rubbed her back.

Saying during the council's annual general meeting while looking directly at a female staff member that he would "get his whip out" to try to have the council's annual report given to elected members more quickly.

Telling another staff member to "stick to your knitting and get back to the kitchen" during a council workshop.

Using the phrase "like a n***** in the woodpile" at a council workshop.

Requiring a female staff member to give him her personal phone number "in a way that made her feel as if she had no choice but to comply with his demand" and contrary to council policy.

Putting his arm around a female staff member's waist when she was showing him a form he needed to complete.

Standing "unnecessarily directly behind" a female staff member while she was showing him some information on her computer. The panel said the staff member felt "trapped against the desk".

Seizing the name badge of a female employee "from where it was clipped to her clothing on her chest when she introduced herself to him".

Putting his hands on a female employee's shoulders and physically turning her around to see what was written on the back of her work shirt at a community barbecue.

The panel said Ald Ridler "continued to behave inappropriately and in breach of the code" even after telling the council's acting chief executive during a meeting in December 2024 that he was "clear on the issues raised" and that he would not continue those behaviours.

Some elements of the complaint, including allegations that Ald Ridler bullied staff members and that he breached sections of the code relating to expressing personal views, were dismissed.

The panel determined that Ald Ridler's use of phrases such as "I'll get the whip out", "get back to the kitchen" and "n***** in a woodpile" were not "expressions of personal views" but rather "his patterns of speech".

The complaint was made by the council's former CEO Tony McMullen. (Supplied: GCC)

'A lack of awareness of proper conduct'

The panel said it determined Ald Ridler's behaviour, in addition to breaching the code of conduct, exhibited a "lack of awareness of proper conduct in modern Australian society, particularly in the workplace".

It said Ald Ridler had "exhibited a wilful disregard for the advice given him" by the acting chief executive.

The panel also noted that another alderman had spoken to Ald Ridler about his behaviour with staff, and that the behaviours had been raised in a phone call to the acting chief executive from the deputy mayor.

"The panel reasonably concludes that Ald Ridler's behaviour was causing concern within the elected member group, as well as within the staff," the report reads.

Glenorchy council knocks back merger idea from Hobart Tasmania is a small place with many councils, 29 in fact. A proposal to merge Hobart with neighbouring Glenorchy has been knocked back with the latter saying it would be too costly and there's no community support for it.

During the hearing on May 27, 2025, Ms Mason as chair outlined the procedures to be followed and a summary of what was being investigated.

According to the panel's report, Ald Ridler made a statement outlining the reasons why he believed the hearing should not proceed.

"These included his belief that the hearing was not being conducted under what he termed 'the proper code of conduct'," the report reads.

The panel said Ald Ridler alleged that there was no "uniform code of conduct in Tasmania when the complaint was made" and that "the Glenorchy City Council had no code of conduct in place at the time".

Ms Mason told Ald Ridler that the panel "disagreed with his view on this matter".

Lynn Mason chaired the panel that investigated the complaint against Peter Ridler. (Supplied: Parliament of Tasmania)

"Ald Ridler was invited to continue, but said that he would 'leave it at that', and reminded the panel that he had rights of appeal to a 'higher authority' in the event of an unfavourable determination by the panel," the report reads.

Ridler left hearing before complainant's opening statement

When Mr McMullen was invited to make his opening statement, Ald Ridler said he, his advocate and his support person would leave the hearing because he did not want to "condone what is going on".

Mr McMullen told the panel Ald Ridler had alleged that "council officers had colluded to tarnish his reputation".

"Mr McMullen denied that this was the case," the panel's report reads.

"He noted that where the alleged behaviours had occurred in a public or group context, Ald Ridler had not denied that they had happened, although he did downplay the significance of such behaviour in his response to the complaint.

"Where there were no witnesses to the alleged incidents, Ald Ridler absolutely denied that they had occurred, even though the affected employees had reported the incidents to their supervisor immediately after the event."

The panel found Peter Ridler's behaviour had caused concern "within the elected member group, as well as within the staff". (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

Ald Ridler was first elected to the Glenorchy council in 1987. He lost his seat at the 2014 election, and was re-elected 10 years later. He has served more than 27 years on the council.

The panel said for nine of those years, all Tasmanian councillors and aldermen had been subject to a code of conduct.

While some "slight changes" had been made during the period Ald Ridler was not on the council, the panel assumed he would be "familiar with the code and the need to comply with it".

The sanctions imposed by the panel were a reprimand, a one-month suspension from council duties and a requirement to attend training.

Ald Ridler has been contacted for comment.

The report was dated July 2025, but only made public this week.

title: Heat stroke and stress fractures don't stop teen running 660km for charity
text:
A teenager from Western Australia's South West, travelled more than 2,000 kilometres to the state's north to then run 660km in 14 days.

Lochlan Gilbert lives in Capel, 200km south of Perth, and wanted to raise money to help homeless people as well as give himself a challenge during the school holidays.

So, he chose the Gibb River Road, a 660km stretch in WA's far north that many only travel on with a four-wheel drive.

Lochlan Gilbert's run raised money to help the homeless. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

The 16-year-old spent two months training after school, but admitted more preparation would have been ideal.

Running about 50km a day in 6km bursts, Lochlan started at 4am, resting in the heat of the day, walked when he was fatigued and even crossed rivers on foot.

The Gibb River Road river crossings are well-known among four-wheel drivers. However, Lochlan Gilbert ran the road instead. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

Both his feet swelled up with suspected stress fractures early in the challenge.

"I kind of tried to ignore the fact it hurt quite a bit and I just kind of went into a bit of denial," he said.

"The beauty of doing it on the Gibb is that the closest hospital is about 300 kilometres away, so you don't really have much of a choice other than just to run to the other side."

With daily temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius, Lochlan also got heat stroke on the first day out of Kununurra.

"I fried myself," he said.

Discomfort for a good cause

Lochlan said remembering the cause kept him going when the run became tough.

Lochlan Gilbert ran every day in his school holidays to raise money for homelessness. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

"Obviously, a lot of people who are impacted by homelessness or find themselves vulnerable, they don't really have much of a choice," he said.

"They're kind of forced to have that uncomfortable sort of living standards and so I thought I'd make myself as uncomfortable as possible to help those who aren't fortunate enough to not have a choice in being uncomfortable."

But by the second week, he had found his stride.

"After having some doubts in the first few days, it feels amazing [to be out here]," he said.

"I'm over the moon."

Lochlan Gilbert had to use all his mental strength to get to the finish line of his ultra running challenge. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

The southerner also encountered wildlife up close.

"At the start I was absolutely terrified of hawks, they'd all be circling over me and it got me nervous. I was packing it," he said.

"There's been cattle, wallabies and at night cane toads to avoid stepping on.

"Thankfully, no snakes."

Fundraising a big motivation

He said running through the Wunaamin Miliwundi Ranges, 160km east of Derby, was a highlight despite the hill climbs.

The Gib River Road is famous for its off-road adventures and picturesque views in WA's north. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

"It was my favourite day. The scenery was amazing, a lot of elevation under climb but so worth it. The views were a nice reward," he said.

Lochlan's no stranger to fundraising, having completed a challenge in 2025 to raise money for We Are Mobilise.

"I know where the money's going to go and how impactful it can be for someone," he said.

Lochlan Gilbert had one of his cousins from Meda Station running alongside him in support. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

He got a text message during the run from We Are Mobilise which motivated him further.

"It said when I reached $15,000 I had helped five families," he said.

"It adds fuel to my fire."

He also credited people stopping on the side of the road to encourage him, donate or find out about the cause.

"Dad is on the radio letting drivers know not to be surprised if they see some random kid on the road," he said.

Lochlan Gilbert near Kununurra when the large truck passed him on the Gibb River Road. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

Emotional finish

By the time he crossed the finish line where the Gibb River Road intersected the Derby Highway, he had raised more than $23,000.

Lochlan stopped about 2km from the finish to meet his parents before tackling the final stretch.

"I got ready to kind of head on to that last final stretch and then I reckon I spent probably the first 500 metres of the last 2kms kind of taking it all in and realising what I've done and that I've helped a lot of people in this homelessness scenario," he said.

"It was absolutely unreal coming through the finish."

Lochlan Gilbert had his family as a support crew while he ran 660km along the Gibb River Road. (Supplied: Justin Gilbert)

Now in recovery, there is no rest for Lochlan as returns to high school today.

"I'm definitely going to do something next year," he said.

"Obviously, I'm still raising money for homelessness and going to try to push myself to my absolute limits again."

title: Free nicotine patches on offer to Tasmanian smokers, vapers
text:
A program offering free nicotine patches, as well as gum or lozenges, to Tasmanians trying to quit smoking or vaping has been expanded to cover anyone aged 12 or over.

The monthly package, valued up to $100, will be available to people who reach out to QuitTas for support and who do not have serious complicating health conditions.

QuitTas director Abby Smith said the products will help overcome a cost barrier faced by many Tasmanians and will be provided alongside additional support.

Abby Smith says the program has expanded beyond the initial offering to priority groups. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"When you combine behavioural support plus combination nicotine replacement therapy, like nicotine patches plus an oral product like gum, that actually gives people the best chances of quitting successfully," Ms Smith said.

The products were previously only offered for free to certain priority groups when QuitTas launched the program in July last year, and Ms Smith said she was "thrilled" to expand it to other Tasmanians.

Those priority groups included people aged 12 to 25, new and expecting parents, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and those eligible for a national lung cancer screening program.

QuitTas has budgeted about $144,000 towards the program for the 2026–27 financial year, which it said would support about 400 participants.

The free nicotine products would be given over a 12-week course. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Participant follow-up

Sophie Harris, who quit using nicotine about four years ago, was hopeful the program could help others do the same.

"I definitely think it's going to help, because obviously price plays a big factor in that stuff," she said.

"It will definitely help people see a bit clearer when money is not a problem."

Sophie Harris thinks making the nicotine patches free will encourage smokers and vapers to try them out. (ABC News: Rani Fletcher)

Ms Smith said the free products would be given over a 12-week course, meaning participants could save up to $300 — in addition to what they are saving by not purchasing tobacco or vapes.

QuitTas manager Nyre Harris said counsellors would call participants regularly to check if the products were working and to be "making sure that they're successfully in their journey".

"I just want people to understand that there are different ways to quit. You don't always have to go cold turkey, you can use these products," Ms Harris said.

Nyre Harris says the program would also include follow-up support. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Ms Harris said some of the conditions which could make people ineligible for the free products would include any recent or upcoming surgeries, certain medications and heart problems.

QuitTas said some people with complex medical conditions could still be able to access the products under the guidance of a general practitioner.

Tasmania has the second-highest smoking rate in Australia, with 17.6 per cent of adults smoking either daily or occasionally.

QuitTas counsellor Adam Mitchell said the service had "definitely" noticed an increase in calls from young people looking to stop vaping.

"We understand that quitting can be quite a shame-inducing journey, or smoking in general, so we encourage anyone … to give us a call and we meet them we're there at," Mr Mitchell said.

"They don't even have to be considering actually quitting, but maybe even making a slight change, and we will greet them with warm open arms and follow them along the journey."

The expansion of the program has been facilitated through funding from the Tasmanian government and will run until the end of June 2027.

title: Brisbane 2032 Olympics organising committee chief Cindy Hook to step down
text:
The Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games organising committee will search for a new CEO, with chief executive Cindy Hook announcing she will depart at the end of her contract.

Ms Hook was appointed in December 2022, with her four-year contract set to expire early next year.

In a statement, the organising committee said a search for a new CEO "will commence immediately and an appointment is expected in the coming months".

Ms Hook said she was "grateful" for the opportunity to see the committee "through the first horizon of Games planning".

"During the past four years, I have achieved everything we had hoped for and had many amazing experiences along the way," she said.

Ms Hook was appointed to the role of Brisbane Olympics CEO in 2022. (ABC News)

"The foundations of success have been well laid. This is the right time to hang over to a new CEO for the next phase."

She said she was confident the event would be "a Games that all Australians will be proud of".

"I look forward to seeing the Games Vision brought to life and you can be sure I will be the greatest fan in the stands at the 2032 Games."

'Exceptional leader'

On Ms Hook's appointment in 2022, Brisbane Olympics president Andrew Liveris expressed hopes she would stay in the role until the Games.

"I can already tell you from the board, our mindset is we recruited a CEO for 10 years, health willing, God willing and everything else willing and that's the way we're approaching this," Mr Liveris said in 2022.

Andrew Liveris previously expressed a desire for Ms Hook to stay in the role until the Games. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

The committee shake-up comes as the Games moves from initial planning phase to operational delivery, with venue construction underway.

Mr Liveris said Ms Hook had been an "exceptional leader".

"Cindy commenced when the Organising Committee was a fledgling startup and has transformed Brisbane 2032 into a thriving organisation ready to go to the next level of Games execution," he said.

"Her focus on values, organisational excellence and strict financial and governance processes are embedded throughout a high calibre team that she recruited and I thank her for her great contributions."

Five years since Brisbane secured the Olympics Broken promises and scarcely broken ground. Five years since Brisbane secured the 2032 Olympic Games, this is the state of play.

Speaking in state parliament, Queensland sports and Olympics minister Tim Mander thanked Ms Hook for her "dedication, professionalism and service".

"Cindy has played an important role in the foundation building phase and now Brisbane 2032 is moving into a period increasingly focused on procurement, operations, project delivery and event readiness," he said.

"I wish Cindy, her family and her future endeavours every success and thank her for the remarkable contribution she has made to Queensland, to Australia and the Olympic and Paralympic movement."

Federal sports minister Annika Wells said Ms Hook had played a vital role in the development of the Games.

"The work she has done is incredibly valuable and Brisbane 2032 will continue to build on her achievements as Queensland and Australia gets ready to host the world," Ms Wells said.

As Beth Mooney prepares to join illustrious company, she hinted that the allure of a home Olympics could prolong her career and those of her fellow veterans, as cricket vies to defend its looming Games berth for Brisbane 2032. On Wednesday, when the third one-day international against Bangladesh begins at Allan Border Field in Albion, Mooney will become the 10th woman to reach the 100-game milestone – an accolade shared with teammates Ellyse Perry (170) and Megan Schutt (113). The former Brisbane Heat star landed on the radar after her family moved from Victoria to Hervey Bay, where her elite catching and natural batting talent caught the eye. Now, of those to reach a century of caps, she trails only Meg Lanning for batting averages (53.51 versus 49.81). Beth Mooney has risen from humble regional Queensland roots to become a great of Australian cricket. Getty Images “It’s pretty amazing, and a good opportunity to reflect on what’s been sometimes challenging, but a lot of fun for a period of time in my life,” said Mooney, who has averaged less than 40 with the bat in the 50-over format in just three of her 11 years as an international cricketer (2016, 2020, 2024).

Norfolk Metals has shaken up its board, installing new leadership to drive a strategic pivot towards becoming a significant copper player in Chile’s mineral-rich fields. The company has appointed respected mining executive Anthony McClure as executive chairman, effective immediately. A geology graduate of Macquarie University, he brings more than 35 years of technical, management and financial experience in the global resources sector, including board roles with Strickland Metals, Gateway Mining and Silver Mines. Anthony McClure, newly appointed executive of Norfolk Metals. Geologist Richard Pugh has joined as a non-executive director. He holds a degree in exploration and resource geology from Cardiff University, has more than 18 years of industry experience and is chief executive of Gateway Mining. He previously served as executive technical director and non-executive director at Strickland Metals and worked as a senior consulting geologist and exploration manager for several resources companies. The pair now join non-executive director Leonardo Pilapil, following the departure of executive chairman Ben Phillips, who had served as a director since July 2021.

Advertisement

‘Norfolk’s transformational acquisition of the Ciclón Copper Project offers the perfect opportunity to reposition the Company’ Norfolk Metals executive chairman Anthony McClure The board refresh signals Norfolk’s intent to execute its proposed “transformational” acquisition of the Ciclón copper project in northern Chile. The deal, comprising US$45 million (A$67.5 million) in cash and US$5 million (A$7.5 million) in shares, would propel Ciclón into the spotlight as Norfolk’s flagship asset and cornerstone of its copper ambitions. The project sits in Chile’s world-class Domeyko Cordillera copper belt, a postcode that hosts behemoth mines including Collahuasi, Chuquicamata and La Escondida. It hosts an impressive JORC-compliant resource of 11.8 million tonnes grading 2.88 per cent copper equivalent: 8 million tonnes in the higher-confidence indicated category at 2.93 per cent, and 3.8 million tonnes inferred at 2.80 per cent. The polymetallic deposit contains credits of copper, zinc, lead, silver and gold. Ciclón is particularly compelling because of its advanced stage. The brownfields asset comes with more than 40,000m of historical drilling, a 2021 feasibility study and permits for three underground mining operations, alongside a processing plant and tailings facilities. Norfolk Metals executive chairman Anthony McClure said: “The reported JORC Resource highlights the quality and scale of the Ciclón Copper Project and reinforces our view that this is a compelling acquisition opportunity for Norfolk.”

To fund the acquisition and subsequent exploration, Norfolk plans to raise between A$100 million and A$120 million. Once the deal is done, management plans to hit the ground running with a proposed 53,000-metre drill campaign across its Chilean portfolio. While Ciclón is set to be the main event, Norfolk also holds the Carmen copper project in Chile’s Atacama region. A maiden drilling campaign there last year returned encouraging results, including a 53m intercept grading 1.1 per cent copper from 62m. Carmen offers a dual-track opportunity, with a near-surface oxide copper blanket potentially suited to heap-leach processing and deeper sulphide potential. As part of its sharpened focus on Chile, the company has shed its legacy assets. Its Roger River exploration licence in Tasmania expired in August and Norfolk now holds no ground in the state. title: Is Australia prepared to cope with its 'modern-day success story'?
text:
IN BRIEF: Emergency departments will increasingly struggle to cope with an influx of elderly patients, a new report has found.

Experts say that older people are falling through the cracks at every level of the health and aged care systems.

Australians are living longer and the healthcare system is increasingly unable to cope, according to a new national report on the state of emergency departments (EDs).

The Australasian College of Emergency Medicine's (ACEM) third annual report notes that while Australia's ageing population is a "modern-day success story", the nation is not sufficiently prepared for the influx of elderly people into EDs.

From 2019 to 2024, the number of older people attending EDs increased by 16 per cent, compared with a 4 per cent increase among younger people, with half of all elderly presentations to an ED resulting in a hospital admission.

The group also found disparities in hospital care requirements between groups of older people.

While all non-Indigenous people aged 65 years and over were significantly more likely than younger people to be classified in higher urgency categories, arrive by ambulance and be admitted into hospital, that also holds for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 years and over.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

ACEM president Dr Peter Allely said EDs were "far from ideal" environments to treat elderly patients, due to their "harsh lighting, loud noises and constant interruptions".

"We see too many frail people made afraid, confused and unwell by an unfamiliar environment, far away from their loved ones, familiar faces, supports and home comforts."

He said that, despite the "scale and predictability of demographic trends", governments across Australia had done little to prepare for the "volume and complexity of care needs" for the ageing population.

As a result, significant pressure was now being felt at "all levels" of the health system, including hospitals, primary and aged care facilities, and in-home support programs, he added.

ACEM is the organisation responsible for training emergency medicine specialists and setting standards for emergency care in Australia and New Zealand.

Across-the-board lack of preparedness

University of New South Wales professor in ageing health Lee-Fay Low agreed, saying she didn't think Australia had been doing anything long-term to prepare the health system for Australia's ageing population.

Similarly to Allely, Low said this lack of preparedness wasn't unique to hospitals, but could also be seen in primary care clinics, aged care facilities, and even among families.

Low, who is also leader of the Ageing and Health Research Group at the University of Sydney, said the ongoing aged care crisis was affecting people's ability to receive preventative care.

"Right now, because you have to wait for aged care, those things that might help might prevent you from going to emergency, like poor nutrition, ending up with an infection because your hygiene's not looked after."

READ MORE Aged care giant refunds $200,000 to residents over disputed living fees

Even since the Royal Commission into Aged Care handed down its final report in 2021, lengthy waitlists for aged care providers have seen many people go without crucial care, Low said.

"After the Aged Care Royal Commission, the government released more home care packages, allowing people to age in place without going into nursing homes. But that waitlist is a year long again now.

"The problem is that with the aged care reforms, things are worse now ... I mean, waiting a year is ridiculous.

"People living in their homes aren't really getting that aged care in a timely way, and that precedes these emergency visits."

READ MORE What 720 Australians reveal about ageing well — and the key to longevity

New health department data released yesterday found an average of 17 older Australians died while waiting to receive support at home care each day last year — an increase of more than a third on the previous year.

As of June 30, more than 106,000 Australians were on the official waiting list for a place in the Commonwealth-funded Support at Home program, while the ABC's Four Corners reported in August that the true number of people waiting was almost 154,000.

'Urgent action' needed

Older Australians made up only 17 per cent of the population in 2024 but accounted for almost a quarter of all ED presentations.

The ACEM report said that, without "urgent action", increased ED presentations by older people would disproportionately impact the healthcare system.

Using population growth modelling from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the report projected a 177 per cent increase in total ED presentations between 2010 and 2050, noting projected increases of 242 per cent for people aged 65 to 84, and 411 per cent for people aged 85 and over.

ACEM is calling for federal, state and territory governments to urgently improve the quality of care older people receive across the health system, reduce ED demand, lift hospital capacity and provide sustainable hospital care for all Australians.

The government's latest Intergenerational Report projected rapid population ageing and falling fertility rates would fundamentally reshape the economy and budget out to 2065–66. By 2030, nearly one in five Australians will be aged 65 and over.

"The ratio of working people to older people is going to change substantively," Low said.

Allely warned that "Australia's health system and its health workforce are just not equipped for this demographic change."

More funding not the only remedy

Low said preparing for an ageing future required more than a funding boost.

"We always say we should have more funding, but I think where the funding is focused is important."

She also said proper reform would also require "an adjustment in presumptions and expectations Australians have for care as they get older".

"I think the presumption and the expectation in Australia is that when you get older, if you need care, you've paid taxes your whole life and the government will look after you. And that's already untrue, right? Aged care doesn't look after you straight away."

Low said a "national conversation" was needed to identify where the responsibility for care lies — whether it is with the government, or a co-contribution arrangement through which "as part of saving for retirement and super, that we also put aside some money, if we need help and we can pay for care".

Reforms also need to ensure the aged-care sector has a sufficient workforce, one-third of which is currently made up of migrants. Australia needs to reconsider decisions made around cutting migration, Low said.

She also suggested more families needed to start conversations about the "expectation that maybe mum and dad will need some help, and at that stage we might have to work less or chip in somehow to support the care".

But beyond families, she said, "this is not a conversation that we've had nationally".

title: Hackers hit French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food
text:
In brief The refrigeration control systems of Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted in the attack.

The incident comes amid growing concern over potential havoc that can be caused in Europe by malicious cyberattacks.

Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50C overnight, causing fires and spoiling food.

The Paris prosecutor's office said on Tuesday (AEDT) that a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France", leading to food losses and fires.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a spokesperson in his office said.

France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk.

Félix Aimé, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 stores in France, said 5 per cent of its stores were affected.

Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarché, said fridges at around 150 of its stores were heated up to 50C for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said staff discarded all affected food to eliminate health risks.

Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff at an Intermarché in central Paris throwing whole carts of defrosted frozen foods into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street.

READ MORE Why we're still living with password rules their creator regrets

Dominique Schelcher, the CEO of Coopérative U — a collective of independent hypermarkets and supermarkets — said his group had also been targeted.

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X.

There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarché CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the "unprecedented" attack would represent losses amounting to "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day".

Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said: "This incident underlines the importance of resilience across the entire supply chain."

Cold aisles controlled via internet

Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store's fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere.

The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.

Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems".

The affected units "were running outdated firmware", Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions".

The attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a dozen US military commissaries in late August that led to food losses after fridges were affected.

Dutch retailer also reports 'cybersecurity incident'

Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize AD.AS, which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a "security issue" on its network and had taken several systems offline as a precaution.

A message on the retailer's smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a "cybersecurity incident".

Online orders account for about 10 per cent of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news agency ANP reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders.

Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets.

Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying "site temporarily down".

It was unclear whether other operations had been affected.

title: The surprising health condition some people develop after moving to Australia
text:
In brief Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

For some migrants, hay fever doesn't appear until years after they move to Australia.

Zoe had never experienced hay fever before moving to Australia.

But a few years after arriving, she began experiencing red and itchy eyes. At first, she assumed they were a reaction to her contact lenses.

When the symptoms worsened and returned year after year, she started looking for another explanation.

Along with itchy eyes, she said she developed severe nasal congestion and an urge to sneeze. After seeking medical advice, she was told she had hay fever.

"It took me years to realise," Zoe, who asked for her last name to be withheld for privacy reasons, told SBS Thai.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Allergic rhinitis, commonly known as hay fever, occurs when the immune system reacts to airborne allergens. Common triggers include pollen, dust mites, mould and animal dander (flakes of skin in fur, hair or feathers).

Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

For some migrants, the condition only emerges after several years of living in the country, with research suggesting exposure to new environmental allergens may play a role.

Why allergies can emerge years after migration

Dr Jason Yu, a Sydney-based general practitioner and clinical allergist, became interested in allergy medicine after moving between countries. He had not experienced allergies as a child but developed them years later.

He said allergies can develop at any stage of life, although they often first appear in childhood.

"We don't know the exact reasons why people develop allergies," Yu told SBS Thai.

One possible explanation for developing new allergies after migration is exposure to a novel environment, which can introduce people to allergens they hadn't previously encountered.

Yu said dust mite allergies are common in Sydney and other coastal areas, while grass pollen, including ryegrass pollen, was another prominent trigger in Australia.

"Pollen can be blown kilometres away," he said.

Pollen is a key trigger of hay fever. Source: AAP / Tracey Nearmy

Yu said there isn't yet a definitive explanation for why some people develop allergies and others don't.

Genetics and the development of the immune system may also play a role. Infections can also influence immune responses, although their relationship with allergy development is complex.

Research has previously documented the development of allergic conditions among people who migrate to Australia.

A 1996 study found up to 60 per cent of people who moved from South-East Asian countries to Australia developed hay fever, while 15 per cent developed asthma within their first 10 years in Australia.

A 2015 study from Curtin University also reported similar findings, suggesting people who migrated from China were more prone to allergies after moving to Australia.

For Hansa, whose last name has been withheld for privacy reasons, the first signs of hay fever were easy to mistake for a cold.

"One day, all of a sudden, my nose wouldn't stop running, my eyes were watering, and I kept sneezing," she told SBS Thai.

While living in Thailand, Hansa occasionally reacted to construction dust, but she hadn't experienced the same symptoms after moving to Australia.

About three years after her arrival, the symptoms began.

She had assumed that if she was allergic to something, the reaction would appear straight away, rather than emerge several years after the move.

Antihistamines are commonly used to manage hay fever, but Yu said the ideal form of treatment depends on a person's symptoms.

For those whose main symptom is nasal congestion, corticosteroid nasal sprays may be more effective than antihistamines alone, he said.

For persistent or more severe allergies, allergen immunotherapy may also be an option.

When hay fever becomes more serious

Hay fever and asthma are different but closely related conditions.

Hay fever primarily affects the eyes and upper airways, while asthma affects the lower airways and causes symptoms such as wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.

"If you feel short of breath, you feel like heaviness on your chest, you definitely should see someone about it," Yu said.

He said this was particularly important because, in rare circumstances, exposure to grass pollen can trigger a potentially life-threatening event known as thunderstorm asthma.

Asthma can cause severe breathing difficulties, raising the potential risks for undiagnosed persons. Source: AAP / Tracey Nearmy

Under certain weather conditions, storm outflows can concentrate grass pollen into smaller particles. When inhaled, those particles can penetrate deeper into the lungs, triggering inflammation and narrowing airways.

"It doesn't happen often, but if it does happen, it has really deadly consequences," Yu said.

Melbourne experienced what's considered the world's largest recorded epidemic of thunderstorm asthma in November 2016. Thousands of people developed breathing difficulties, placing significant pressure on the city's emergency services and hospitals.

The event also highlighted the disproportionate impact thunderstorm asthma can have on some migrant communities.

A study published by The Lancet in 2018 found people of Asian or Indian ethnicity were disproportionately impacted, representing 39 per cent of people who attended hospital. Six of the 10 who died were of South or Southeast Asian ethnicity.

Hay fever and asthma can also occur together, and Yu said some people may not realise they have both conditions.

"I've had a few patients come in; they didn't realise they had asthma as well; they thought they just had hay fever.

"But because I checked, I could actually identify they actually have asthma."
