title: The country coming for a $20-billion Australian export market
text:
IN BRIEF: Brazil is the world's leading beef exporter and producer.

Commentators warn that shifts in global markets could see the country absorb Australia's markets.

Australian beef could face its toughest competition yet, as the world's leading producer encroaches on its traditional export markets.

Since the early 2000s, Brazil has consistently ranked as the world's leading beef producer, with an enormous 230 million-strong herd in 2024, more than the country's estimated population. The South American country is also the world's leading exporter, sending its beef to 130 different countries.

Australia has long prided itself on its beef exports: in 2025, 1.5 million tonnes of beef were sent to 83 countries. In 2025, the value of Australian beef exports was $19.6 billion, according to Australia's red meat research and marketing body, Meat and Livestock Australia (MLA).

But commentators are suggesting South American exporters are expanding in Australia's most important export markets — South Korea and Japan — which could have significant impacts on price competition over the coming months.

Speaking on a recent agribusiness podcast, Angus Gidley-Baird, senior animal proteins analyst at food and agribusiness bank Rabobank, said Australia’s beef sector should closely monitor developments in Brazil.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Over the past few years, we’ve seen Brazil increase its presence in several of Australia’s export markets," Gidley-Baird said.

"Combined with changing trade dynamics involving China, the United States and Europe, it is becoming increasingly important for Australian producers and exporters to understand what is happening in the Brazilian beef sector."

Brazil already has a big presence in the Australian meat industry, through worldwide giant JBS. It's the biggest meat processing company in Australia, owning a series of foodlots and abattoirs, as well as the smallgoods company Primo Foods.

More than half of Brazil's beef exports are to China, and it hit its annual quota of 1.1 million tonnes for shipments to the country last month.

China's commerce ministry said it would start collecting an additional 55 per cent tariff on Brazil's beef shipments on 1 October after the South American country reached its annual ‌quota of 1.1 million tonnes.

Rabobank Brazil animal protein analyst Wagner Yanaguizawa said that new quota restrictions significantly reduced Brazilian shipments during the second half of 2025, creating surplus volumes that would need to be redirected elsewhere, and could translate into greater competition for Australia in alternative destination markets.

Australia exported beef to 83 countries in 2025. Source: Getty / Darren Hunt / FlickrVision

Yanaguizawa said the United States was likely to absorb some of the displaced volume, while the Middle East, Indonesia, Vietnam, Chile and the United Kingdom also presented opportunities. Those markets would not be sufficient to offset reduced Chinese demand, though, he said.

Yanaguizawa said the potential opening of Japan and South Korea to Brazilian beef also warrants close attention from Australian industry participants.

"Japanese and South Korean inspections of Brazilian processing plants had been completed, and final reports were pending before market access decisions could be finalised. Industry expectations are that access could be granted later this year," Yanaguizawa said.

"These two markets are very important for Australia, and soon Australia may have a new competitor," he said.

READ MORE The $1 billion problem facing Aussie farmers like Robert

The MLA is aware of the shift. On an August 2026 podcast, the corporation's regional manager for Southeast Asia, Valeska, said that as global trade patterns shifted, Australian beef volumes had been redirected from China into Southeast Asia.

At the same time, competition across Southeast Asia was intensifying, as exporters from South America actively pursued new opportunities across the region.

"The South Americans are really active and quite aggressive. At the [World Food Expo in the Philippines] yesterday, we spoke with Brazilian packers who indicated they're looking at alternative markets."

Valeska said she believed Australia's long-term investment in Southeast Asia positioned the industry well.

"We're not resting on our laurels. Australian beef is definitely ramping up activities across Southeast Asia, and I think it's an opportunity to really secure the premium segment while continuing to grow demand through other channels."

title: Josh Frydenberg says 'things have to change' as he questions Liberal leadership
text:
In brief Former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg has criticised Angus Taylor's leadership of the Liberal Party.

He told Nine's 60 Minutes that 'things have to change' after Liberal polling fell to an all-time low.

Angus Taylor would welcome the political return of Josh Frydenberg to parliament, despite the former treasurer attacking his leadership of the Liberal Party.

Frydenberg used an interview to criticise Taylor's handling of the party, saying the current leader had contributed to Liberal polling being at an "all-time low".

"Things have to change, because there's something existential about the threat that I think the party now faces," he told Nine's 60 Minutes on Sunday night.

"[Taylor is] getting [criticism] from lots of corners. People are saying that the Liberal Party needs to do better."

The latest Newspoll had the Coalition's primary support at 20 per cent, compared to Labor's 29 per cent and One Nation's 26 per cent.

Excerpts from Frydenberg's memoir, which is likely to contain policy suggestions, have fuelled rumours that he is planning to make a political comeback.

"Look, I certainly haven't closed the door, but I don't need to rush to a decision. The next election is 18 months away," he said.

Despite the criticism, Taylor said his former Liberal colleague would be welcomed back into the fold should he decide to run.

The Liberal Party's fortunes have not improved after Angus Taylor took over as leader in February. Source: AAP / Bianca de Marchi

"I welcome every Liberal who cares about the future of our nation — and I know Josh does — to put shoulder to the wheel in the coming months to get rid of a rotten Labor government and make the change that Australia needs happen," he told reporters in Canberra on Monday.

"I ask all Liberals and Nationals and people who are supportive of our view about where the country needs to go … to get in there and help in any way they can."

Frydenberg held the Melbourne seat of Kooyong for 12 years from 2010 and was treasurer in the Morrison government, including through the COVID-19 pandemic.

He lost the seat to independent MP Monique Ryan at the 2022 election, in which she won almost 53 per cent of the two-party preferred vote.

Ryan appeared unfazed by her competition's possible return.

"I'm not bothered either way," she told Nine's Today program.

"Josh does have a track record with the Kooyong community."

"He was the member for that seat for 12 years, and in 2022, our community rejected him because they were so frustrated with his inability to affect any change to government policy on climate change.

"People were unhappy with his economic management."

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson has encouraged others to put themselves forward as Liberal candidates. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson encouraged people to "put themselves forward" as candidates to create a stronger Liberal Party.

"I encourage them to do so, so they can be part of a winning team. So we can have an Angus Taylor-led government," he told ABC Radio.

"What we need is people who've got courage in their hearts and are prepared to make the sacrifices necessary for public office."

title: Should you be paid to exercise while at work? These Australian researchers think so
text:
IN BRIEF: Physical inactivity costs the Australian economy $2 billion annually, the Heart Research Institute says.

Researchers believe the introduction of exercise while at work could have significant health outcomes.

Should workers get paid exercise breaks? It's a question Australian researchers are asking in an upcoming trial, as they track health outcomes and productivity for shift workers given time to exercise on the job.

Researchers believe targeted measures to address physical inactivity could improve Australia's cardiovascular health, mental health, and physical wellbeing.

Heart disease is a key health issue in Australia, with more than one million Australians aged 18 and over (6.4 per cent of the adult population) living with one or more conditions related to heart, stroke or vascular disease in 2024, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

Regular exercise can reduce the risk of heart disease by up to a third, while helping to lower blood pressure, improve cholesterol levels, and strengthen the heart muscle.

The Heart Research Institute says physical inactivity costs the Australian economy over $2 billion annually.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Cardiologist Dr Faraz Pathan says physical inactivity is a "costly exercise", and that scale-able solutions are needed.

Physical inactivity "leads to a burden of cardiovascular disease and mental health issues", he said, and the increased risk of developing cancers.

"That means we lose staff to absenteeism. We lose people to illnesses. We lose people to the premature truncation of their careers," he told SBS News.

"Amplified at the level of society and economy, this is a very costly exercise."

Dr Faraz Pathan (centre) says scale-able solutions are needed for physical inactivity. Source: SBS News

For nurse Lisa Barry, who has three children, exercise fell down the priority list as life got busier.

"You get home from work absolutely exhausted, and the last thing you feel like doing is exercising," she told SBS News.

"So having it as part of your workday would be fantastic."

Lisa is one of 100 healthcare workers at Nepean Hospital in western Sydney who will be given 30-minute exercise breaks during their shifts for the upcoming study, with activities including walking, boxing, and virtual reality tennis.

'The intervention is not actually exercise'

The trial, led by the Heart Research Institute, is set to begin next year.

"The intervention is not actually exercise," Pathan said.

"It is the time, the opportunity in your workday to exercise, so you get back home, you can be a mum or a dad, look after your elderly parents."

Pathan says having hospital shift workers as study participants presents unique challenges that researchers will be looking to tackle.

"Why a hospital? Because I think shift work is a significant cardiometabolic risk factor — we have a large proportion of shift workers — but so is physical inactivity, so is chronic stress.

"I do think doing a trial like this in hospital is doing it on hard mode, because there are competing priorities.

"But if we can pull it off in this group, and if we show that people are doing better, well then I would love to see this implemented in businesses and in environments across Australia.

"My dream is for Australia to be the first country that brings this into existence for workers.

'We've led the world in public policy before, so I think we can be ambitious."

The 12-month study aims to examine whether exercising on the clock improves staff cardiovascular health.

Researchers will compare the results of participants who were given exercise breaks at the start of the 12 months with those who receive them 6 months later.

Researchers looking for broader wellbeing benefits

Pathan says the study will track changes in heart health and fitness, but that researchers will carefully look for any differences in overall wellbeing, including mental health.

"Is depression improved? Is burnout improved? Is anxiety improved?

"Because I think some of the benefit may not only be cardiovascular. It may actually be in your mental health and wellbeing as well."

Pathan believes small amounts of exercise built into the working day can make a huge difference over time, and if the study is successful, he said he hopes the idea could be rolled out to workplaces around the country.

Lisa Barry says exercise breaks could improve her energy levels and productivity.

"I think it'll be good for a mental reset," she said.

"And then you come back, and you're ready to go, you're hyped up, you're ready to keep on going with your shift.

"I think it'll have that effect of 'let's finish this shift, let's get through the day'."

title: 'You better think again': Hanson names Liberal leader she'd prefer over 'smarmy' Taylor
text:
IN BRIEF Yesterday, Hanson said the Opposition leader and another Liberal leadership hopeful were unfit to lead the party.

On Saturday, she said Angus Taylor was a "smarmy management consultant" and Tim Wilson was "full of himself".

One Nation's Pauline Hanson has revealed her pick to head right-wing counterparts the Liberals after dismissing its current leader as a "smarmy management consultant".

Angus Taylor became the first sitting Opposition leader to address the Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Brisbane on Saturday as the Coalition and One Nation vied for the fractured right-wing vote.

But Hanson emerged the crowd favourite as she made jibes about her conservative rivals while also offering to "put personal history aside" and team up with the Coalition to remove Labor from government.

title: Coalition defends migration cuts on economic grounds, rejects One Nation-style bans
text:
In Brief Coalition says cutting migration to 100,000 would lift productivity by prioritising higher-skilled workers.

Taylor rejected One Nation-style country bans, saying migrants should be judged on conduct and character.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has defended the Coalition's proposed migration overhaul as an economic reform designed to boost productivity, while rejecting the idea of banning migrants based on their country of origin.

The Coalition's plan would cut net overseas migration (NOM) to 100,000, about a third of current levels, while increasing the share of "high-value" migrants entering Australia.

They have called it the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history".

However, Taylor's comments to ABC's Insiders on Sunday also appeared to mark a shift in tone from his last appearance on the show.

This time, he repeatedly framed the changes as an economic measure aimed at boosting productivity and competitiveness, rather than focusing on national security or cultural concerns.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Taylor highlights migration plan as economic reform

Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.

"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.

"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.

"It will raise productivity, it will raise competitiveness, it will raise the average income of the people coming into this city."

Taylor said the policy would increase the average skill level of migrants entering Australia while reducing overall numbers through changes to a range of visa programs, including student, graduate and bridging visas.

He repeatedly argued migration settings should be geared towards lifting productivity rather than simply increasing population growth.

"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone," he said.

Bringing in more highly skilled migrants would put downward pressure on inflation because it would raise productivity, Taylor argued, saying "this is pretty simple economics".

The Coalition plans to dramatically cut temporary visa holders under their proposed migration policy. Source: SBS News

"When you bring someone to Australia, you are bringing demand and supply. If that person is low-skilled, you are bringing more demand than supply. If they are high-skilled, you are bringing the opposite, actually bringing more supply.

"One of the reasons why we've had a collapse in productivity in this country ... is that our immigration program has not been working to drive up our productivity and it should be."

He also defended the Coalition's proposal to halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 places, saying "charity begins at home" and such measures were designed to "balance the budget".

Taylor distances Coalition from One Nation approach

While much of Taylor's defence of the policy focused on economics, he also sought to draw a distinction between the Coalition's approach and proposals advanced by One Nation.

The comments marked a different emphasis from Taylor's previous appearance on the same program in April, when he argued migrants from "bad countries" posed a higher risk to Australia.

Pressed at the time on which countries he considered "bad", Taylor pointed to Iran and referred to security concerns involving people arriving from Gaza.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Asked on Sunday why the Coalition had not gone as far as One Nation in proposing immigration restrictions based on nationality, Taylor rejected the comparison.

"I've always said we will discriminate not based on the country someone comes from or their race or their religion, but based on the person and whether that person is a suitable person to be a resident or citizen of this country," he said.

"That's what we should focus on, and we should judge people on their character and conduct, not the colour of their skin."

Taylor maintained that some countries could present higher risks for security agencies to assess.

"It is true that risks are higher where there is a bad regime — there is no question about that."

"That doesn't mean screen them all out. That means make sure you are assessing those risks appropriately."

One Nation has previously proposed measures targeting migration from specific countries, including pausing new migration from countries subject to a federal government 'do not travel' warning.

However, Taylor also linked the Coalition's migration policy to a broader focus on screening prospective visa holders.

"People who do not believe in our system of law, people who do not believe in our basic freedoms, they shouldn't be coming to this country," he said.

"If they've got here on a visa, they should be thrown out."

Later on Sunday, other Coalition figures reiterated those sentiments, following reports that the flydubai co-pilot accused of attempting to hijack a flight bound for Israel was allegedly radicalised while studying in Melbourne.

Opposition home affairs spokesperson Jonno Duniam said there was no place for "hate preachers who spread extremism, glorify terrorism or encourage violence".

"That is why the Coalition will tighten visa laws to keep those who preach hatred out of Australia and deport non-citizens who promote violent extremism," he said.

“At a federal level, we also need stronger visa screening, better intelligence sharing and properly resourced counter-terrorism agencies. That is why the Coalition has committed to establishing an Enhanced Screening Coordination Centre to bring together our intelligence, policing and border protection capabilities."

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Australia had its toughest-ever powers to prevent violent extremists entering the country.

"I've been using them to be able to scan and assess whether someone has a history of being a problem before we give them a visa, and we've been cancelling visas when people are here, and we've been stopping people from coming here in the first place," he told News24 on Sunday.

The economic debate over immigration levels

Taylor's argument rests on the idea that a smaller, more highly skilled migration intake would boost productivity while reducing pressure on housing and infrastructure.

However, the economic impacts of migration cuts remain heavily debated among economists, migration experts, business groups and policymakers.

Critics argue lower migration can reduce labour supply, tax and visa revenue, population growth, consumer spending and business activity, particularly in industries that rely heavily on migrant workers.

A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education.

The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.

Debate over migration's impact on housing has also intensified in recent years. While higher migration can increase demand for homes, some experts argue migrant workers are also needed to address labour shortages in the construction sector.

In September, Burke said migration cuts would inevitably come with economic trade-offs and warned no industry would be immune from their effects.

"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he told SBS News.

"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure — as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."

Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.

One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which they say will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.

title: 'Open the gates': Hellas boss calls for A-League admission after stunning final win
text:
in brief The South Melbourne Hellas have won the Australia Cup for the first time.

The 1-1 final came down to a penalty shootout in front of a sold-out crowd on Saturday night.

South Melbourne FC's co-president has said the nation's A-League might be knocking on his team's door after it became the first National Premier Leagues (NPL) side to win the Australia Cup, beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in an emotionally charged blockbuster final.

In one of the greatest nights in Australian domestic football history, former National Soccer League (NSL) powerhouses South first took Victory to extra time, then fought back from 1-0 down to level it at 1-1 at the death before winning 4-3 on penalties in front of a pumping sellout crowd of 29,911 fans at the Melbourne Rectangular Stadium.

It was the biggest moment in 22 years for South, commonly known as the Hellas, a reference to Hellenic (the native Greek name for Greece) to honour the large post-war Greek-Australian community that founded and supported the club.

The team was locked out of top-flight football alongside other NSL clubs when that league folded in 2024, and has long craved an A-League licence.

Bill Papastergiadis, South Melbourne FC's co-president, is confident his squad's performance on Saturday night will strengthen their chances of being granted entry to the nation's top tier of football.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We will be knocking on the A-League's door, or is the A-League knocking on South's door? Not sure what it is at the moment."

"Football needs to open the gates to allow clubs like South in and bring the passion back."

Those sentiments were echoed by the club's coach, Sinisa Cohadzic.

"I really cannot find any excuse not to see this club to play in the A-League," Cohadzic said.

"You talk about the A-League, the resources that they have and we have — it’s probably on par, and that’s why our players are able to compete."

South Melbourne captain Marco Janković said: "If you were someone that is in Europe [with] no idea what clubs they were, you wouldn’t know who's the A-League team — I think that’s something we noticed and it's very special".

'Surpasses even the most beautiful dreams'

South's stunning win came after Cohadzic urged his players to seize their chance in their 54th game this season, after losing the OFC Pro League final to Auckland FC.

"I said to them that tonight sometimes the reality surpasses even the most beautiful dreams, and tonight was one of those nights," he said.

"It was one of those nights where they had to believe that they can get a result."

Denis Genreau scored an athletic, improvised half-volley in the 95th minute to put Victory in front, before Max Mikkola forced home an equaliser in the 117th minute to send the game to penalties and the crowd into ecstasy.

In the penalty shootout, South Melbourne goalkeeper Javier Lopez was the hero and won the Mark Viduka Medal as man of the match.

Lopez initially saved former South captain Harrison Sawyer's penalty but was ruled to have come off his line — but then saved the re-take too.

"I remember in January when the club said we want to win the Australia Cup. I said 'you guys, that would be crazy'," Lopez said.

"Now we are the champions."

South scored all their penalties before Victory skipper Jason Davidson, son of South Melbourne great Alan Davidson, hit his must-score spot-kick over the bar.

In becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup, South have succeeded where Heidelberg last year and Sydney United 58 in 2022 could not.

With the win, South also technically claim a berth in next season's Asian Champions League 2 competition.

The defeat also extends Victory's silverware drought, with the club's most recent trophy the 2021 Australia Cup.

South certainly played up to the occasion, taking the game to Giovanni Savarese's Victory and making their mark on their biggest night in years in an incredible atmosphere.

A huge contingent of their fans packed the south end of the stadium, holding banners of club legends including Ange Postecoglou, Ferenc Puskás and John Margaritis.

"You guys have stuck with us for 20 years, playing in the NPL and you've shown tonight what this future holds for this great club," Janković said.

The only lowlight of the night was a section of the crowd at the South end booing the Welcome to Country before the match.

Victory should have taken the lead in the 78th minute when Santos' poor shot allowed Lopez to make an extraordinary save with his knees.

But there was nothing Lopez could do in extra-time to stop himself being lobbed by Genreau's strange half-volley, which bounced over the line before he could grab it.

Then, with the clock winding down, South substitute Jordan Swibel burst down the right and sent in a ball that caused chaos and ended with Mikkola toe-poking home.

Hellas fans erupted and when the game was sent to penalties minutes later, only one club ever felt on top.

"We were not surprised by the stadium, by the environment ... it was a proper Australia Cup the way it should be," Savarese said.

"I think it will be remembered as one of the most iconic.

"Unfortunately, on our side, I wish we lifted the trophy."

— With additional reporting by Adrian Arciuli

As more than 60,000 students sat down for the first HSC exams of 2026, English Paper 1, many were braced for the ultimate curveball: an essay question based on an extract from the student’s prescribed text. “We were all expecting a trick … they were freaking out a little bit,” said Yvonne Spiers, an English teacher at Strathfield Girls High School. She, too, had a bad case of pre-exam jitters, admitting she did not sleep the night before. Strathfield Girls High School HSC English exam students Laila Graham, Stephani Chow and Serina Surti said the exam was easily adaptable to their prepared responses. I think our girls will do it really well.”

The relief began in section one, where students were asked to answer short questions based on unseen text. In the first question, students were provided an extract from Lang Leav’s collection of poetry and micro-essays Soon It Will Be Sunday, a work discussing a storm battering a manuka tree. Students were asked how Leav invites readers to consider the human quality of resilience. It’s the very beginning [of the HSC] but I am going to get through all of this. I could draw on my own feelings and experiences to answer the question.” In another question based on an unseen text, students were asked to compare attitudes towards success. Stephani Chow, 17, said she wrote about how success is not defined by titles or accumulations of objects. “It’s defined by your character and how you end up feeling after being successful,” she said. In section two of the exam – a 20-mark essay – students were asked how the author of their prescribed text “offered opportunities to examine assumptions about human strength and vulnerability”.

Her students having studied Arthur Miller’s The Crucible, Spiers said they were primed for success. “The good answer will be that basically The Crucible explores the complexity between the two – there is no such thing as showing strength without having shown vulnerability first.” Spiers said the question was “definitely easier than the short text but even the short text was accessible. Laila Graham, 18, agreed. “It wasn’t anything out of the blue. It’s just new text, new questions. You’re just applying the techniques, your pre-memorised quotes, and you just go,” she said. As Beth Mooney prepares to join illustrious company, she hinted that the allure of a home Olympics could prolong her career and those of her fellow veterans, as cricket vies to defend its looming Games berth for Brisbane 2032. On Wednesday, when the third one-day international against Bangladesh begins at Allan Border Field in Albion, Mooney will become the 10th woman to reach the 100-game milestone – an accolade shared with teammates Ellyse Perry (170) and Megan Schutt (113). The former Brisbane Heat star landed on the radar after her family moved from Victoria to Hervey Bay, where her elite catching and natural batting talent caught the eye. Now, of those to reach a century of caps, she trails only Meg Lanning for batting averages (53.51 versus 49.81). Beth Mooney has risen from humble regional Queensland roots to become a great of Australian cricket. Getty Images “It’s pretty amazing, and a good opportunity to reflect on what’s been sometimes challenging, but a lot of fun for a period of time in my life,” said Mooney, who has averaged less than 40 with the bat in the 50-over format in just three of her 11 years as an international cricketer (2016, 2020, 2024).

“It’s hard to believe 100 games have passed, but I’m proud of what the team has achieved in that time, the journeys we’ve been on in different groups, and the role I’ve played in that success along the way. “I like to think I’m pretty level when I play my cricket, I don’t get too up or too down, but I also can’t take too much of the credit. Norfolk Metals has shaken up its board, installing new leadership to drive a strategic pivot towards becoming a significant copper player in Chile’s mineral-rich fields. The company has appointed respected mining executive Anthony McClure as executive chairman, effective immediately. A geology graduate of Macquarie University, he brings more than 35 years of technical, management and financial experience in the global resources sector, including board roles with Strickland Metals, Gateway Mining and Silver Mines. Anthony McClure, newly appointed executive of Norfolk Metals. Geologist Richard Pugh has joined as a non-executive director. He holds a degree in exploration and resource geology from Cardiff University, has more than 18 years of industry experience and is chief executive of Gateway Mining. He previously served as executive technical director and non-executive director at Strickland Metals and worked as a senior consulting geologist and exploration manager for several resources companies. The pair now join non-executive director Leonardo Pilapil, following the departure of executive chairman Ben Phillips, who had served as a director since July 2021.

‘Norfolk’s transformational acquisition of the Ciclón Copper Project offers the perfect opportunity to reposition the Company’ Norfolk Metals executive chairman Anthony McClure The board refresh signals Norfolk’s intent to execute its proposed “transformational” acquisition of the Ciclón copper project in northern Chile. The deal, comprising US$45 million (A$67.5 million) in cash and US$5 million (A$7.5 million) in shares, would propel Ciclón into the spotlight as Norfolk’s flagship asset and cornerstone of its copper ambitions. The project sits in Chile’s world-class Domeyko Cordillera copper belt, a postcode that hosts behemoth mines including Collahuasi, Chuquicamata and La Escondida. It hosts an impressive JORC-compliant resource of 11.8 million tonnes grading 2.88 per cent copper equivalent: 8 million tonnes in the higher-confidence indicated category at 2.93 per cent, and 3.8 million tonnes inferred at 2.80 per cent. The polymetallic deposit contains credits of copper, zinc, lead, silver and gold. Ciclón is particularly compelling because of its advanced stage. The brownfields asset comes with more than 40,000m of historical drilling, a 2021 feasibility study and permits for three underground mining operations, alongside a processing plant and tailings facilities. Norfolk Metals executive chairman Anthony McClure said: “The reported JORC Resource highlights the quality and scale of the Ciclón Copper Project and reinforces our view that this is a compelling acquisition opportunity for Norfolk.”

To fund the acquisition and subsequent exploration, Norfolk plans to raise between A$100 million and A$120 million. Once the deal is done, management plans to hit the ground running with a proposed 53,000-metre drill campaign across its Chilean portfolio. While Ciclón is set to be the main event, Norfolk also holds the Carmen copper project in Chile’s Atacama region. A maiden drilling campaign there last year returned encouraging results, including a 53m intercept grading 1.1 per cent copper from 62m. Carmen offers a dual-track opportunity, with a near-surface oxide copper blanket potentially suited to heap-leach processing and deeper sulphide potential. As part of its sharpened focus on Chile, the company has shed its legacy assets. Its Roger River exploration licence in Tasmania expired in August and Norfolk now holds no ground in the state. Its Orroroo uranium project in South Australia is also considered non-core and is under review for a potential joint venture or divestment. The corporate team has also been strengthened, with solicitor Sleiman Majdoub appointed joint company secretary alongside Arron Canicais. Majdoub brings corporate, commercial and legal experience, including advising mining explorers and supporting listed companies with reporting and compliance. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
